item.description: What allowed occultism to blossom in the United States at the turn of the 20th century? Linotype machines, cheap pulp paper, and newly improved postal networks. Allan Johnson investigates the forgotten history and (still living) world of mail-order magic.

item.title: Pulex irritans: The Attack of the Monster (1885)
item.description: Lantern slide of man battling bug.

item.title: “A Beautiful Purplish Hue”: Frank Dudley Beane’s Experience with Ergot and Cannabis Indica (1884)
item.description: An early contribution to drug literature, in which a man came to be fashioned out of wood.

item.title: Introducing PDR Press Minis
item.description: Announcing an exciting new book series!

item.title: Broken Ground: The Fall of the House of Usher (1928)
item.description: A modernist adaptation of Edgar Allan Poe. One of the first avant-garde films from America.

item.title: Songs from the Commons: A Q&A with Simon Close about the Public Song Project
item.description: The creator of WNYC's Public Song Project on creativity, copyright, and the public domain.

item.title: The Great Majority: Body Snatching and Burial Reform in 19th-Century Britain
item.description: As populations flocked to city centres in the 19th century, church cemeteries began to overflow with the dead. Roger Luckhurst exhumes the history of this period, when anatomists fuelled a body-snatching trade led by “resurrection men” and reformers sought alternatives to the toxic urban graveyards and their pestilent fumes.

item.title: Elizabeth I’s Manuscript Copy of Pierre Boaistuau’s Histoires Prodigieuses (1559)
item.description: Marvels, wonders, and monstrosities: something between a medieval bestiary and a scientific treatise on birth defects.

item.title: “Wretches, Speak Evil of Me”: Goethe and Schiller’s Xenions (1896 edition)
item.description: One of the most elaborate works of literary insult ever written.

item.title: Doing Impressions: Monet’s Early Caricatures (ca. late 1850s)
item.description: Moneymaking caricatures by a teenage Monet, before he turned to Impressionism.

item.title: Fear and Fragility: The Glass Delusion and Its History
item.description: In early modern Europe, around the time when lenses began to bring the world (and heavens) into newfound focus, patients started appearing in medical records with a particular ailment: a firm belief that they were made of glass. Tamara Sanderson investigates the source and manifestation of this delusion, and finds a psychological idiom that once carried the weight of what could otherwise not be…

item.title: Calicornication: Postcards of Giant Produce (1909)
item.description: "Tall-tale" or "exaggeration" postcards illustrating the bounties of California.

item.title: Charlotte Perkins Gilman’s Herland (1915)
item.description: A utopian novel where men are no longer necessary.

item.title: Wayang Kulit: Raden Soelardi’s Illustrations of Javanese Puppets (1919)
item.description: Illustrations of Javanese wayang kulit puppets with vivid colour and gilding.

item.title: The Blinkered Flâneur: Walking with Franz Hessel in 1920s Berlin
item.description: Does the flâneur , that curiously modern figure who wanders metropolitan streets, have a political consciousness? For Franz Hessel — author of Spazieren in Berlin , “a memorization while strolling” that Walter Benjamin called “thoroughly epic” — the answer seemed to be no. Paul Sullivan explores Hessel’s perambulations through Berlin and the achievements and limitations of his vision.

item.title: Unbridled Passions: The Eight Horses of King Mu, Son of Heaven (ca. 1300)
item.description: Unruly steeds from King Mu’s mythology, cavorting across a silk scroll.

item.title: Pigeons Transmogrified: Hannah Glasse’s Art of Cookery (1751 edition)
item.description: A bestselling 18th-century cookbook, containing the first recipe for curry in English.

item.title: Snail Homes, Bog Bodies, and Mechanical Flies: Robert Testard’s Illustrations for Les secretz de l’histoire naturelle (ca. 1485)
item.description: A wondrous illuminated manuscript, which gathers and illustrates the marvels of the world and beyond.

item.title: Sekka Zusetsu: A Book of Snowflakes (1832)
item.description: Observations of “snow flowers” made by microscope in Edo-era Japan.

item.title: Typing for Love or Money: The Hidden Women’s Labor behind Modern Literary Masterpieces
item.description: Taking dictation, revising manuscripts, typing copies, literary amanuenses often labour for little compensation and even less recognition. Christine Jacobson explores the neglected efforts of women like Theodora Bosanquet, Véra Nabokov, and Valerie Eliot, who — through their work as typists, editors, and champions — had a profound impact on modern literature.

item.title: Sara Weiss’ Journeys to the Planet Mars (1903)
item.description: A forgotten bridge between Spiritualism and UFO encounters.

item.title: Autobiography of a “Jeep” (1943)
item.description: A WWII propaganda film narrated as an "auto"-biography

item.title: Cybernetic Attention: All Watched over by Machines We Learned to Watch
item.description: Before the attention economy consumed our lives, “pursuit tests” devised by the US military coupled man to machine with the aim of assessing focus under pressure. D. Graham Burnett explores these devices for evaluating aviators, finding a pre-history of the laboratory research that has relentlessly worked to slice and dice the attentional powers of human beings.

item.title: Flights of Fancy: The Nine Birds of Jacques de Fornazeris (1594)
item.description: Etchings of birds in a somewhat theatrical style.

item.title: A Prophet of the Weather: Lantern Slides by Clement Lindley Wragge (ca. 1900–22)
item.description: Slides from twenty years of lecturing about the workings of the universe and the fate of the soul.

item.title: Peter Kropotkin’s Memoirs of a Revolutionist (1899)
item.description: The memoirs of an aristocratic man revolutionised into an anarchist communist.

item.title: Happy Public Domain Day 2026!
item.description: Each January 1st is Public Domain Day, when a new crop of works have their copyrights expire and become free to share and reuse for any purpose. Here's our highlights for 2026.

item.title: Top 10 Most Read Pieces from 2025
item.description: From sublime spheres to hungry cats, a rundown of the ten most read of what we published this year.

item.title: A Thousand and One Nights in Italy: The Moorish Fantasias of Cesare Mattei and Ferdinando Panciatichi
item.description: In mid-19th century Italy, two eccentric aristocrats set forth on parallel projects: constructing ostentatious castles in a Moorish Revival style. Iván Moure Pazos tours the psychedelic chambers of Rochetta Mattei, optimised for electrohomeopathic healing, and Castello di Sammezzano, an immersive, orientalist fever dream.

item.title: Nature Morte: Chaïm Soutine’s Still Lifes (ca. 1920s)
item.description: Still lifes by the artist who seemed to bridge expressionism with the baroque.

item.title: Deceit and Disrobing: The Schefer Maqāmāt (BNF Arabe 5847, ca. 1237)
item.description: Illustrations of Abū Zayd and his adventures in double meaning.

item.title: Luke Howard’s Essay on the Modification of Clouds (1865)
item.description: First cloud taxonomer and a poem by Goethe.

item.title: The Launch of Our End-of-Year Fundraiser!
item.description: Our End-of-Year Fundraiser is launched, and the new postcards theme will be Attention.

item.title: “Quaint Dessert Dishes” in American Homes and Gardens (1911)
item.description: Bizarre sweet treats that resemble human and animal forms.

item.title: Henri Rivière’s Thirty-Six Views of the Eiffel Tower (1888–1902)
item.description: French lithographs of the Eiffel Tower and its environs, in the style of Japanese woodblock prints.

item.title: Art in Art: Cabinets of Curiosity and the Rise of the Gallery Painting
item.description: In the 17th century, emanating from Antwerp, a new genre of artwork came on the scene: paintings of paintings, works populated by a lush array of meta-images. From its origins in picturing private curiosity cabinets to its later use in documenting increasingly public collections, Thea Applebaum Licht charts the course of this alluring aesthetic tradition.

item.title: Too Computerised? Too Cold?: 1999 A.D. (1967)
item.description: A past vision of the future. Domestic utopia? Or sanitised hell?

item.title: New T-Shirts (Now in 100% Organic Cotton) and New Mugs in Our Shop!
item.description: Adorn your body and coffee in PDR goodness! We’ve just added 8 new T-shirts and 13 new mugs to our online shop.

item.title: Roma Lister, Aradia, and the Speculative Origins of a Witchcraft Revival
item.description: In 1899, Charles Godfrey Leland published Aradia , “the gospel of the witches”, containing a goddess-orientated creation and saviour narrative, purported to descend from an ancient, hermetic tradition of witchcraft in Italy. A. D. Manns explores this text via an enchanting conjecture: that the writer, medium, and witch Roma Lister played a pivotal role in the formation of both Aradia and,…

item.title: Last Order Dates for the Holiday Season - 2025
item.description: The recommended cut-off dates to order from our shop by to ensure delivery in time for Dec 25th.

item.title: Perverse, Grotesque, Sensuous, Inimitable: A Selection of Works by Aubrey Beardsley
item.description: Selections from an artist whose phantasmagoric works defined an era.

item.title: Animal Costumes from the 1862 Fairytale Ball of the Jung-München Artist’s Association
item.description: Photographs from a costume ball featuring fairytale fables.

item.title: PDR's Halloween Reader
item.description: This Halloween week, a devilish dive into our archives to unearth some supernatural treats...

item.title: “That’s Why We Become Witches”: Sylvia Townsend Warner’s Lolly Willowes (1926)
item.description: A novel about a woman who throws off the yoke of patriarchy to become a witch.

item.title: Hooked on Sonics: Experimenting with Sound in 19th-Century Popular Science
item.description: Of all the senses cultivated throughout the 19th century, it was the sense of hearing that experienced the most dramatic transformation, as the science of sound underwent rapid advancement. Lucas Thompson delves into a particular genre of popular acoustics primers aimed at children and amateurs alike, which reveal the pedagogical, ludic, and transcendental strivings of Victorian society.

item.title: A Treatise on the All-Healing Qualities of Earth Bathing (1790)
item.description: A medical tract on the health effects of burying oneself alive in mud.

item.title: Paramaribo and the Plantation: Gerrit Schouten’s Dioramas of Suriname (1810–30)
item.description: Dioramas avant la lettre that depict local life in Suriname.

item.title: The Nature of the Beast: Charles le Brun’s Human-Animal Hybrids (1806)
item.description: Illustrations of supposed physiognomic affinities between humans and animals.

item.title: The Adventures and Experiences of the First Slovak Novel
item.description: Partially banned upon publication and translated into English for the first time this year, René, or: A Young Man’s Adventures and Experiences (1783–85) found new readers in the communist era thanks to its critiques of feudalism, capitalism, and the Catholic Church. Dobrota Pucherová introduces us to this hybrid work, which mixes the bildungsroman with the philosophical novel, the romance, the…

item.title: Vertiginous Accounts: Travels in the Air (1871 edition)
item.description: Expedition accounts of aeronauts bravely venturing into the heavens on hot-air balloons.

item.title: Birth of the Pearl (1901)
item.description: A "living picture" film staging Botticelli’s Birth of Venus with a twist.

item.title: The End of the World as We (Didn’t) Know It: Now and Then #5
item.description: A Rapture that wasn’t, in 2025 and 1844.

item.title: The Shadow of Desire: Painting the Origins of Art (ca. 1625–1850)
item.description: Paintings illustrating Pliny the Elder’s account of the origins of art.

item.title: “You Think Me a Bold Cheat”: Mary Carleton, Counterfeit Princess
item.description: Accused of posing as foreign royalty to lure her young suitor into a bigamous marriage, Mary Carleton was the subject of dozens of pamphlets and broadsides published in the mid-17th century, including by Carleton herself. Investigating the fraudster’s life, Laura Kolb finds a self-fashioning figure who both influenced the emergence of the English novel and serves as a strange precursor to our…

item.title: A Collection of Old English Customs, and Curious Bequests and Charities (1842)
item.description: A compilation of historical gifting traditions in England, with a focus on the peculiar.

item.title: Ivan Aivazovsky’s Miniature Seascapes (ca. 1887)
item.description: Identical photographs of the artist, each with a unique miniature painting at the centre.

item.title: The Cat’s Maew: Thai Treatise on Auspicious Felines (19th Century)
item.description: A manuscript that pairs illustrations of cats with poetic descriptions and notes on what mystical benefits their owners might hope to accrue.

item.title: Watching the World in a Dark Room: The Early Modern Camera Obscura
item.description: Centuries before photography froze the world into neat frames, scientists, poets, and artists streamed transient images into dark interior spaces with the help of a camera obscura. Julie Park explores the early modern fascination with this quasi-spiritual technology and the magic, melancholy, and dream-like experiences it produced.

item.title: Cannibal Modernity: Oswald de Andrade’s Manifesto Antropófago (1928)
item.description: A modernist manifesto inspired (controversially) by the Tupi people of Brazil.

item.title: Flowers of Fealty: Wilhelm Dilich’s Commemoration of the Christening of Elisabeth of Hesse (1598)
item.description: Commemorative manuscript featuring illustrations of pageants, costumes, and fireworks, later further illustrated by a separate artist, with floral motifs.

item.title: Breaking the Celestial Ceiling: Now and Then #4
item.description: Female astronomical first, in 2025 and 1787.

item.title: Through the Magnifying Glass: The Cheese Mites (1903)
item.description: A trick film in the peepshow vein, involving magnification and mites on a block of cheese.

item.title: Splitting Hairs: Chinese Immigrants, the Queue, and the Boundaries of Political Citizenship
item.description: As Chinese immigration to California accelerated across the 19th century, the hairstyle known as the queue — a long, braided pony tail — became the subject of white Americans’ fascination, disgust, and legal regulation. Sarah Gold McBride explores why hair served as an index of political subjecthood, and how the queue exposed cracks in American norms regarding gender, economy, and citizenship.

item.title: The Mowing-Devil (1678), or, the Earliest Known Depiction of a Crop Circle
item.description: A crop circle sighting tinged with Christian morality.

item.title: Perspiration, Bilocation, and Plagiarisation: “The Heat Wave” (1929)
item.description: Time travel and murder during a New York heat wave.

item.title: The “Private” Photographs of Bolette Berg and Marie Høeg (ca. 1895–1903)
item.description: Excerpts from a dazzling image collection, discovered in a Norwegian barn in the 1980s, that experiments with the presentation of gender.

item.title: Dancing Naked on the Head of a Pin: The Early History of Microphotography
item.description: In 1853, John Benjamin Dancer achieved a feat of seemingly impossible scale: he shrunk an image to the size of a sharpened pencil tip. Anika Burgess explores the invention of microphotography and its influence on erotic paraphernalia and military communications.

item.title: Trojan Pig: Tiny Cryptic #11
item.description: Eleventh instalment in our series of extremely small and free-form cryptic crossword puzzles, themed on our latest essay.

item.title: The Language of Form: Lothar Schreyer’s Kreuzigung (1920)
item.description: The sole example of a Bauhaus workshop’s arcane theatrical scoring system, combining colours, words, and complex symbolic notation.

item.title: Strings Attached: Helen Haiman Joseph’s A Book of Marionettes (1920)
item.description: The first comprehensive history of marionette artistry in the English language.

item.title: Off with Their Heads: Illustrations of Blemmyes (ca. 1175–1724)
item.description: Depictions of the mythical creatures known as Blemmyes: humanoids whose eyes, nose, and mouth are embedded in their breast.

item.title: Imagining an Idle Countess: George Wightwick’s The Palace of Architecture
item.description: In 1840, British architect George Wightwick published a world history of architecture in the Romantic mode, inviting readers to enter a vast garden where Buddhist iconography rubs shoulders with Greek temples and Egyptian pyramids gaze upon Gothic cathedrals. His intended audience? Idle women. Matthew Mullane revisits this visionary but ultimately unpopular text, revealing the legacy of attempts…

item.title: Under Construction: Tiny Cryptic #10
item.description: Tenth instalment in our series of extremely small and free-form cryptic crossword puzzles, themed on our latest essay.

item.title: Drawing on Tradition: Elena Izcue’s Peruvian Art in the School (1926)
item.description: A set of drawing workbooks embroiled in debates about the Indigenist aesthetic movement.

item.title: Charles Davy’s Conjectural Observations on the Origin and Progress of Alphabetic Writing (1772)
item.description: A series of conjectures about the primal scene of writing.

item.title: Bernard Sleigh’s Anciente Mappe of Fairyland (ca. 1920 edition)
item.description: A stunning six-foot-long map that joins the worlds of various myths and stories for the childhood adventurer.

item.title: The Old, Old, Very Old Man: Thomas Parr and the Longevity Trade
item.description: As the story goes, Old Tom Parr was relatively healthy for being 152 until a visit to noxious, polluted London in 1635 cut his long life short. Katherine Harvey investigates the early modern claims surrounding this supercentarian and the fraudulent longevity business that became his namesake in the 19th century.

item.title: Old Tricks: Tiny Cryptic #9
item.description: Ninth instalment in our series of extremely small and free-form cryptic crossword puzzles, themed on our latest essay.

item.title: “The Great Enigma of Our Times”: Henry George’s Poverty and Progress (1881 edition)
item.description: A landmark work of social reform — proposing a land value tax — that helped usher in the Progressive Era.

item.title: In the Penal Colony: Now and Then #3
item.description: French overseas imprisonment, in 2025 and 1852.

item.title: Gilded Fish: Illustrations from Histoire naturelle des dorades de la Chine (1780)
item.description: Stunning illustrations from the first monograph on goldfish published in Europe.

item.title: Charles Butler’s The Feminine Monarchie, or the History of Bees (1634 edition)
item.description: The earliest full-length work of apiculture published in English, which popularised the discovery that bee colonies have queens instead of kings.

item.title: As Bright as a Feather: Ostriches, Home Dyeing, and the Global Plume Trade
item.description: In the 19th century, dyed ostrich feathers were haute couture, adorning the hats and boas of fashionistas on both sides of the Atlantic. Whitney Rakich examines the far-reaching ostrich industry through a peculiar do-it-yourself-style book: Alexander Paul’s The Practical Ostrich Feather Dyer (1888), a text interleaved with richly colored specimens.

item.title: Warburg’s Werewolf: An Anamnesis
item.description: Aby Warburg spent his life finding forms that could hold their own against the flow of time. All the while, as Kevin Dann explores, he was churning on the brink of madness with the sense that he himself was changing — into a terrifying animal. What kind of history would a werewolf write?

item.title: Mudpots and Fumaroles: Lithographs of Yellowstone’s Thermal Springs (1883)
item.description: Images gathered during a survey by Ferdinand V. Hayden, who was responsible for the designation of Yellowstone as a national park.

item.title: Feather Tickler: Tiny Cryptic #8
item.description: Eighth instalment in our series of extremely small and free-form cryptic crossword puzzles, themed on our latest essay.

item.title: A Popeless Situation: Now and Then #2
item.description: Papal elections begin, in 2025 and 1268.

item.title: Tangled Dürer: The Six Knots (ca. before 1521)
item.description: Woodcut knots likely inspired by Mamluk decorative metalwork.

item.title: Nikolai Agnivtsev’s Little Screw (1925)
item.description: A 1925 Soviet Children’s book about a little screw whose importance is overlooked.

item.title: Confessional Boxes: Tiny Cryptic #7
item.description: Seventh instalment in our series of extremely small and free-form cryptic crossword puzzles, themed on our latest essay.

item.title: “I Am Making the World My Confessor”: Mary MacLane, the Wild Woman from Butte
item.description: In 1902, a woman named Mary MacLane from Butte, Montana, became an international sensation after publishing a scandalous journal recording life at the age of 19. Rereading this often-forgotten debut, Hunter Dukes finds a voice that hungers for worldly experience, brims with bisexual longing, and rages against the injustices of youth.

item.title: Oskar Kokoschka, Hermine Moos, and the Alma Mahler Doll
item.description: Photographs of the life-size doll that Kokoschka had made to resemble his ex-lover Alma Mahler.

item.title: Afoot
item.description: In 2004, the world’s foremost scholar on Sherlock Holmes was found garrotted on his bed. Richard Lancelyn Green had been planning a three-volume biography of Arthur Conan Doyle but had had trouble gaining rights to the author’s private papers and manuscripts, which were scheduled to be auctioned at Christie’s. Lancelyn Green believed that Doyle’s daughter had wanted these to go to the British…

item.title: One World
item.description: Al-longs, ong-fong der lar Part-ree-e-yer, Ler joor der glwore ait arr-ee-vay. — Lyrics to La Marseillaise rendered in phonetic French for British soldiers in World War I, from Frank Scudamore’s “Parley Voo”!! , 1915 (via Tony Augarde’s Wordplay , 2011)

item.title: Help Wanted
item.description:
In an 1893 textbook , criminologist Hans Gross tells how investigators interpreted this ideograph, which had appeared on the wall of a remote Austrian chapel:
The bird, drawn with a single stroke, represents a parrot, alluding to the great loquacity of the owner of the mark, who was famous housebreaker. The second sign is a church, the third a key. Below, we see three round objects on a line;…

item.title: Ha!
item.description:
In 1722, Jonathan Swift published the “last speech” of one Ebenezer Elliston, “a malefactor executed for street robbery,” “published at his desire for the common good”:
Now as I am a dying man I have done something which may be of good use to the public. I have left with an honest man (and, indeed, the only honest man I was ever acquainted with) the names of all my wicked brethren, the…

item.title: Mouthful
item.description: In 1641, a syndicate of Puritan clergymen published a pamphlet upholding the Presbyterian theory of the ministry. They published it under the memorable pseudonym Smectymnuus, an acronym derived from the initials of the five authors: Stephen Marshall, Edmund Calamy, Thomas Young, Matthew Newcomen, and William Spurstowe. The Oxford English Dictionary still recognizes the wonderful word …

item.title: Paper Route
item.description: Image: Wikimedia Commons Origami can solve general cubic equations! The method was developed by Italian mathematician Margherita Piazzolla Beloch, who in 1936 found a way to use paper folding to construct the common tangents to two parabolas. Given two points p 1 and p 2 and two lines l 1 and l 2 , we can, whenever possible, make a single fold (dashed line) that puts p 1 onto l 1…

item.title: The Social Whirl
item.description: In a 1962 nightmare , writer Thomas Meehan imagined having to introduce Uta Hagen to Yma Sumac, Ava Gardner, Abba Eban, Oona O’Neill, Ugo Betti, Ona Munson, Ida Lupino, the Aga Khan, Ira Wolfert, Ilya Ehrenburg, and Eva Gabor at a Greenwich Village cocktail party: “Uta, Yma; Uta, Ava; Uta, Oona; Uta, Ona; Uta, Ida; Uta, Ugo; Uta, Abba; Uta, Ilya; Uta, Ira; Uta, Aga; Uta, Eva.” Then Polish…

item.title: Before and After
item.description: Why does the slogan ‘Whatever is, always was to be’ seem to imply that nothing can be helped, where the obverse slogan ‘Whatever is, will always have been’ does not seem to imply this? We are not exercised by the notorious fact that when the horse has already escaped it is too late to shut the stable door. We are sometimes exercised by the idea that as the horse is either going to escape or not…

item.title: Long Distance
item.description: The Javan cucumber, Alsomitra macrocarpa , broadcasts its seeds on papery wings that can glide long distances. Some have been found on the decks of ships. The unique design inspired aviation pioneer Igo Etrich to build an artificial flying wing, which he adapted into Germany’s first mass-produced military aeroplane.

item.title: The Watercolor Illusion
item.description: The interior of this map is white, but it appears to be suffused with a pale yellow. In fact the blue and orange coloring is confined to the border. This “bleeding” effect was discovered by University of Sassari psychologist Baingio Pinna in 1987. It’s still being investigated.

item.title: Photo story: finding adventure in Reno Tahoe
Scientists develop breakthrough potential cure for hepatitis B
Blood, poop and carcasses: How feasting bugs are helping map biodiversity
item.description: Critters that dine on flesh and waste also consume the animal’s DNA. That genetic material is helping scientists detect and map elusive species and their pathogens.

item.title: How to tame AI’s voracious appetite for energy
item.description: Scientists are exploring new algorithms, hardware and computing methods to lower AI’s power demands. Strategic siting of data centers and other steps to increase green energy use are also key.

item.title: They call it stupid hot for a reason: Heat muddles animal brains
item.description: As temperatures rise, some creatures pick fights while others struggle to learn. The consequences of these behavioral changes may ripple through ecosystems.

item.title: A social compass in the brain
item.description: People with a rare genetic disorder that damages the amygdala are helping neuroscientists rethink how the brain shapes fear, trust and concern for others

item.title: A revolutionary cancer treatment could transform autoimmune disease
item.description: Researchers are testing CAR T cell therapy as a way to reset the immune system in lupus, Graves’ disease and other conditions where the body’s defenses go rogue

item.title: The Power of Play
item.description: In this monthly issue, we take a closer look at how games, imagination, and creative experimentation shape identity and culture.

item.title: Why your brain loves games — and how to use that to your advantage
item.description: I remember sitting in class as a kid, struggling to pay attention while my teacher explained fractions. But at home, I could play Age of Empires for five hours straight — managing civilizations, balancing economies, and fighting wars on multiple fronts. The games I played demanded serious thinking, planning, and problem-solving. And yet they never felt like work. The cognitive effort was…

item.title: Why play brings us pleasure
item.description: Since the days of ancient Greece, thinkers have grappled with the mystery of why humans and other animals play. Survival is hard, so why waste energy? Over the years, theories have ranged from Plato’s simple picture of play as skill rehearsal to ever more esoteric ideas about surplus energy, Freudian catharsis, and vestigial “primitive instincts.” These days, developmental psychologists…

item.title: What children learn when adults aren’t around
item.description: Children, like all mammals, are born completely dependent on adults for survival. The primary task of childhood is to grow increasingly independent of this care, and so they are also born with instinctive drives to practice independence to the degree that they can. The most powerful of these is the drive to play. In play, children learn the most important lessons in life, lessons of personal…

item.title: How playgrounds reinvented childhood
item.description: Fictional though they are, Tom Sawyer and Huckleberry Finn exemplify a lost truth about American kids up until the 1880s: Childhood was wild . Like millions of their real-life contemporaries, the protagonists of Mark Twain’s comic masterpieces roamed unsupervised across town and country, looking for fun and adventure, often finding trouble and danger. Then came the Progressive Era and one of…

item.title: The hidden cost of taking yourself too seriously
item.description: I was in St Albans, England, walking through the sunny park leading up to the cathedral, when I saw a small boy rolling down the hill in the grass. I felt something unexpected: jealousy. I wish that were me. Followed immediately by a second thought: Why couldn’t it be? I could, in theory, roll down that hill. But at what expense? Dirtying my clothes? Looking like a lunatic? In about three…

item.title: Animal play may be about more than survival
item.description: We tend to think of animals as survival machines, their every action designed to help them avoid threats, fulfill needs, and find mates. But what are we to make of a crow that repeatedly places a discarded plastic lid at the top of a snowy roof and then rides it down the pitch like a snowboard? Or orcas that drape dead salmon across their foreheads — a strange behavior that spreads to…

item.title: To access your creativity, start playing
item.description: To live a fulfilling life, we need to have a grasp on our personal values, what lights us up as individuals, and how to connect to ourselves and our communities. Exploring my individual creative expression is my personal favorite way to do all of that. But so many people have buried their creative expression deep inside of them. Did you cringe when you read the term creative expression ?…

item.title: How gamification can ruin your life
item.description: In 2004, I started running. Like some British Forrest Gump, I put on some cheap trainers and went jogging out into the night. But unlike Forrest, I found myself bent over and wheezing into some bushes within minutes. Running is hard if you’ve never done it before. I stuck at it. I put on the same shoes and went out at the same time every evening, and after a while, things got easier. I…

item.title: From Pong to 18 quintillion planets: The evolution of video game play spaces
item.description: Play is a kind of magic. I don’t mean the special-effects-laden spells of wizards, genies, Jedi, and the like, though that can be part of it. I mean a kind of cognitive magic, one that allows us to escape the real world, if only momentarily, and inhabit an imaginative place of our own creation. item.title: Of Thee I Sing
item.description: Image: Wikimedia Commons A set of 4 elements can be partitioned in 15 ways. A poem with 5 lines has 52 possible schemes, corresponding to the partitions of a 5-element set, and so on. These are called Bell numbers .

item.title: Assur: The Supreme God of the Ancient Assyrians
item.description: Assur (also Ashur, Anshar) is the god of the ancient Assyrians who was elevated from a local deity of the city of Ashur to the supreme god of the Assyrian pantheon. item.title: Hara Castle
item.description: Hara Castle was originally built in 1496 as a subsidiary fortification to nearby Hinoe Castle, with upgrades made from 1599 to 1604. Later dismantled and abandoned by the then daimyo (lord) Matsukura Shigemasa (1574-1630), it was briefly occupied by the rebels who took part in the Shimabara Rebellion (1637-38). It now exists as a series of ruins accessible by bus from the city of Shimabara.

item.title: Charvaka: The Ancient Indian Philosophy of Hedonism
